rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request suggests that Paradise is symbolically above Hell.
rows.anchor: suggests that Paradise is situated symbolically above Hell (R, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request conveys the Fire’s terrible heat and thirst.
rows.anchor: indicates the terrible heat and thirst generated by the Fire (R,Ṭs).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The provision requested may mean Paradise drinks such as honey, milk, or wine.
rows.anchor: meaning the other drinks of Paradise (Z), such as honey, milk, or wine

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the provision may mean the food and fruits God gave the Garden’s inhabitants.
rows.anchor: or else the food and fruits that God has provided for them in the Garden (Ṭ, Ṭs, Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request also indicates that hunger is one of Hell’s torments.
rows.anchor: This indicates that hunger is also one of the torments of Hell (R).

rows.speaker: al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: They ask for relief despite despairing that it will be granted, because their circumstances bring confusion and desperation.
rows.anchor: According to al-Zamakhsharī, they ask for relief in this way, even if they despair of it ever being granted to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The requested water may symbolize mercy.
rows.anchor: The water that they ask for can be interpreted as a symbol for mercy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The provision may symbolize the nearness and intimacy with God enjoyed in Paradise.
rows.anchor: that which God has provided may be a reference to the nearness and intimacy with God that those in Paradise have been granted (Su).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both mercy and intimacy with God are denied to those in Hell.
rows.anchor: Both are denied to those in Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers’ treatment of religion as diversion and play is attributed to them elsewhere.
rows.anchor: an attitude attributed to them elsewhere (see 5:57c;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They were also deluded by worldly life.
rows.anchor: and as having been deluded by the life of this world (cf. 6:70, 130;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran elsewhere characterizes this world itself as mere play and diversion.
rows.anchor: for it is this world that is merely play and diversion (6:32;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human forgetfulness of God and moral duties is a recurring Quranic theme.
rows.anchor: forgetfulness of God and of moral obligations is an underlying theme in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran repeatedly urges people to remember God and His commandments or to receive reminders.
rows.anchor: the corresponding and repeated encouragement to remember God and His commandments or to be reminded.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forgotten meeting is Judgment Day, and God’s forgetting them reciprocates their having forgotten it.
rows.anchor: Having forgotten the meeting with this Day of theirs—that is, the Day of Judgment—the disbelievers are themselves forgotten by God; see also 9:67;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reciprocity of forgetting is part of Quranic moral reflexivity, as deceivers are deceived, charity benefits its givers, and evil is requited in kind.
rows.anchor: The reciprocity of “forgetting” and “being forgotten”contributes to the larger theme of moral reflexivity in the Quran

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Forgetting Judgment Day means neglecting to prepare for it through righteous action in this world.
rows.anchor: To have forgotten the meeting with this Day of theirs means to have neglected to prepare for it by acting righteously in this world (R).

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: God’s forgetting them means He does not answer their plea for relief or show them mercy in that way.
rows.anchor: He does not respond to their plea for relief or does not show them mercy in this way (R)

rows.speaker: IK and R
rows.claim: God’s forgetting also means neglecting and abandoning them in their punishment.
rows.anchor: He neglects them and abandons them in their punishment (IK, R).

rows.speaker: Some commentators
rows.claim: God’s forgetting does not mean that the people disappear from His knowledge, since God does not forget in that sense.
rows.anchor: Some commentators argue that God’s “forgetting” them does not mean that such people become absent from God’s Knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Metaphysically, if God forgot anything, that thing would cease to exist.
rows.anchor: if God were to forget anything, that thing would cease to exist.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse means God treats them as though He had forgotten them.
rows.anchor: the verse is understood to mean that God acts toward such people as if He had forgotten them; see 9:67c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image of winds bringing glad tidings before God’s mercy also appears in other verses.

rows.speaker: al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Rain is among God’s most majestic and beautiful blessings.
rows.anchor: which al-Zamakhsharī describes as among the most majestic and beautiful of God’s blessings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Plural winds generally herald Divine Mercy and Bounty.
rows.anchor: The mention of winds in the plural form is generally a sign or harbinger of Divine Mercy and Bounty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Singular wind can instead be a destructive force under God’s command.
rows.anchor: wind in the singular is also invoked in certain verses as a destructive force under God’s command (see, e.g., 3:117;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Heavy clouds portend life-giving rain that revives dead land.
rows.anchor: the heavy-laden clouds portend life-giving rain, reviving a land that is dead

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain reviving drought-stricken land is a metaphor and symbolic proof of human resurrection.
rows.anchor: the revival of drought-stricken lands through rain is offered as a metaphor and a symbolic proof for the resurrection of human beings after their death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because rainstorms can also destroy, the gathering storm warns people to call on God in fear and hope.
rows.anchor: one must always call upon God in fear and in hope (v. 56).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lightning signals a coming storm and rain, and is said to engender both fear and hope.
rows.anchor: where lightning, which also signals a coming storm, and therefore rain, is said to engender both fear and hope

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call to remember concerns resurrection, recalled by reflecting on dead land’s revival.
rows.anchor: That haply you may remember refers to remembrance of the resurrection, remembrance that may be encouraged by reflecting on the revival of dead land.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Pharaoh killed the sorcerers, he let Moses go free.
rows.anchor: Although Pharaoh killed the sorcerers, he allowed Moses to go free.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The notables fear Pharaoh will let Moses and the Israelites live and worship as they choose and abandon Pharaoh’s gods for Moses’ monotheism.
rows.anchor: the Israelites, to live and to worship as they prefer, and to leave you (Pharaoh) and your gods, that is, to abandon the worship of Pharaoh and his gods for obedience to Moses and the worship of the One God

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Some identify Pharaoh’s gods as the sun or sacred cattle, linking this to the Israelites’ calf idol.
rows.anchor: some say he worshipped the sun or certain sacred cattle, hence the Israelites’ inclination to make an idol in the form of a calf in v. 148

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Another view is that Pharaoh was worshipped himself but worshipped no deity.
rows.anchor: Still others assert that Pharaoh was himself worshipped, but did not worship anything himself (Ṭ),

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Another view takes the gods as idols Pharaoh made and ordered people to worship as a way of worshipping him.
rows.anchor: that Pharaoh had made and that he had commanded people to worship as a way of worshipping him (Ṭs, Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The notables’ question may instead mean that Moses’ people had already left Pharaoh and his gods.
rows.anchor: “Will you leave Moses and his people to work corruption upon the earth, when they have left you and your gods?” (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh says he will kill Moses in 40:26, fearing Moses will change their religion or cause corruption by turning people from Pharaoh’s worship.
rows.anchor: where Pharaoh indicates that he will kill Moses himself, fearing that Moses will alter their religion or cause corruption to appear in the land by leading people away from the worship of Pharaoh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat to kill their sons means young sons and spare women, matching Pharaoh’s collective punishments elsewhere.
rows.anchor: that is, their young sons—and spare their women is consistent with his means of collective punishment mentioned elsewhere

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Though Pharaoh spared Moses out of fear of his power, he reportedly carried out the threat against Israelite followers to terrify them and weaken Moses indirectly.
rows.anchor: Although Pharaoh did not harm Moses, out of fear of his great power, he reportedly carried out his threat upon his Israelite followers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qāhirūn is a plural form of qāhir, which is also a Quranic Divine Name or Attribute.
rows.anchor: Dominant translates qāhirūn, a plural form of qāhir, which is a Name or Attribute of God in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s use of language elsewhere reserved for God suggests that he claims divinity and lordship.
rows.anchor: That Pharaoh speaks of himself in terms used elsewhere in the Quran for God alone suggests Pharaoh’s claim of divinity and lordship for himself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Facing Pharaoh’s terrible punishment, Moses urges his people to seek God’s help and be patient, as the Quran generally enjoins help through patience and prayer; God is with the patient.
rows.anchor: Moses advises them to seek help from God (see 1:5c) and to have patience in the same manner that the Quran enjoins believers to seek help in patience and prayer as a general spiritual attitude

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The land refers to Pharaoh’s domain.
rows.anchor: the land, meaning Pharaoh’s domain (R), belongs to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God can make others inherit the land, fulfilled when He gives the blessed eastern and western lands to Israel as a reward for patience.
rows.anchor: and indeed in v. 137 God bequeaths the eastern and western parts of the land that We blessed to the Israelites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that the end belongs to the reverent may mean their Hereafter reward, Israel’s later worldly victory and settlement, or both.
rows.anchor: The end may refer to the reward of the reverent in the Hereafter, to the later worldly success of the Israelites in vanquishing their enemies (v. 129) and settling in the land, or both (R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses was already angry and aggrieved before seeing the people because God told him on the mountain that they had gone astray.
rows.anchor: Moses returned to his people already angry and aggrieved, even before seeing them, because God made him aware of their having gone astray while he was still on the mountain

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asifan can mean sadness as well as intense anger.
rows.anchor: Aggrieved translates asifan, which may connote sadness, but also intense anger (Mw, Ṭ, Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some understand Moses’ anger as directed also at himself for leaving the people.
rows.anchor: but also perhaps at himself for having left them (Mw, Su),

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His grief may concern both the people’s grave error and his departure from intimate discourse with God.
rows.anchor: his grief was both for his people’s grave error and for his having to leave the intimate discourse with God (Mw, Su)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ complaint about the evil course may address all Israelites or their leaders, including Aaron.
rows.anchor: may have been directed at the Israelites generally or at the leaders among them, including Aaron (Z);

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “After me” may mean while Moses was away or after he had set an example of true monotheism.
rows.anchor: after me may mean while Moses was away (IK, Ṭ, Ṭs) or after Moses had set the example of true monotheism (R, Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Command may refer to waiting for Moses’ return; the people were impatient and hastened his return.
rows.anchor: the command that they wait for Moses’ return. It thus addresses their impatience concerning—and their ultimate hastening of—Moses’ return

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ forty-day stay reportedly lasted ten days beyond what the people expected.
rows.anchor: Moses’ forty-day stay upon the mountain was reportedly ten days longer than his people had expected.

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The Command may refer to the people hastening God’s judgment through their actions, a Quranic warning to disbelievers.
rows.anchor: It may also refer to their hastening God’s judgment upon them through their actions (R), a repeated Quranic warning to disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: More broadly, Moses may chastise their impatience about God fulfilling His promise, as he does in the parallel account.
rows.anchor: More broadly, the question might also be meant to chastise them for their impatience regarding God’s fulfillment of His Promise to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses cast down the Tablets in anger and shock, breaking them, as in the Biblical account.
rows.anchor: Moses throws down the Tablets in anger (Ṭ) and shock (Z) upon seeing his people’s idolatrous worship, breaking them (R, Ṭ, Z), as in the Biblical account

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses seized Aaron in anger because Aaron had failed to preserve the Israelites in righteousness.
rows.anchor: He then seizes his brother, Aaron, in anger for his having failed in his charge of preserving the Israelites in righteousness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran gives another account of Moses’ confrontation with Aaron.
rows.anchor: For another narrative of Moses’ confrontation with Aaron, see 20:92–94.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron says “son of my mother” rather than simply brother to evoke Moses’ tenderness and mercy.
rows.anchor: calling him son of my mother, rather than just “my brother,”in a bid to evoke Moses’ tenderness and mercy toward him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron says the people deemed him weak, meaning they no longer recognized his authority, as shown by their following al-Sāmirī and ignoring his pleas.
rows.anchor: meaning that they no longer recognized his authority (R, Ṭ)—as suggested by their having followed instead the directives of al-Sāmirī

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron says the people were prepared to kill him; elsewhere he explains that stronger action might have made him blamed for causing discord.
rows.anchor: and were moreover prepared to slay him; see also 20:94, where Aaron argues that he feared he would be blamed for causing discord among the Israelites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron asks Moses not to let enemies gloat over his further humiliation at Moses’ hands.
rows.anchor: not to let their enemies rejoice in his misfortune—that is, to gloat over his further humiliation at the hands of Moses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron asks not to be classed with wrongdoers, meaning not to be judged guilty of idolatry and punished with the others.
rows.anchor: not to place him with the wrongdoing people, that is, not to consider him guilty of idolatry and so punish him along with the others

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Commentators view Moses’ request for forgiveness as dedication to God and desire for nearness, not an admission of sin.
rows.anchor: is considered by the commentators to be an indication of their complete dedication to God and their desire to draw near to Him, rather than an acknowledgment of sin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This reading reflects the doctrine of prophetic ʿiṣmah, which holds that prophets are immune from sin.
rows.anchor: the prophets are believed to be immune from sin according to the Islamic doctrine of the ʿiṣmah, or “inerrancy,”of the prophets.

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Others say Moses sought forgiveness for his anger and Aaron for not being forceful enough with the Israelites.
rows.anchor: Others suggest that Moses asked God to forgive him for his anger and to forgive Aaron for not being forceful enough with the Israelites

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Neither failing need be considered a serious sin.
rows.anchor: neither of which may be understood as rising to the level of “serious sin.”

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some describe Moses’ anger as holy anger for God, not personal anger.
rows.anchor: Moses’ anger is also said by some to have been not a personal anger, but a “holy anger” for God’s sake

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This holy anger is outwardly manifested as religious wrath, not loss of control.
rows.anchor: rather an anger manifested outwardly, in the form of holy wrath for the sake of religion

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Moses’ inward state remained calm and merciful.
rows.anchor: while Moses’ inner state remained characterized by calm and mercy (Aj).

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: God’s anger may refer to the command that the Israelites atone by “slaying their own” in 2:54.
rows.anchor: is thought by some to be a reference to the command that they atone for their sins by “slaying their own” in 2:54

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some take “slaying their own” to mean killing those Israelites most guilty in the calf incident.
rows.anchor: understand to mean that the Israelites were to slay those among their own people who were most guilty for the calf incident

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others interpret it as collective punishment.
rows.anchor: and others understand as a form of collective punishment; see 2:54c.

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: God’s anger and Israel’s abasement may refer to later hardships suffered by Israelites and their descendants.
rows.anchor: understand both God’s anger and the Israelites’ abasement in the life of this world (see also 2:61) as references to later hardships that were to be suffered by the Israelites and their descendants

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Another view takes God’s anger as punishment in the Hereafter and abasement as future adversity in this world.
rows.anchor: suggest that God’s anger refers to His punishment of them in the Hereafter, while the abasement refers to their future adversity in this world

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Others say Israel’s repentance and atonement meant punishment would occur only in this world, not the next.
rows.anchor: Others argue that the Israelites’ repentance and atonement (in 2:61) meant that their punishment would be only in this world and not in the next

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who fabricate are people who initiate false religious beliefs or practices.
rows.anchor: Those who fabricate refers to those who initiate false religious beliefs or practices

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran repeatedly reminds that God forgives those who truly repent and mend their ways.
rows.anchor: The reminder that God forgives those who are truly repentant and mend their ways is found throughout the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quran 4:17 says God accepts repentance from those who sin in ignorance and quickly turn back.
rows.anchor: God only accepts the repentance of those who do evil in ignorance and then turn quickly in repentance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 7:149 shows that the Israelites’ repentance was quick and unconditional.
rows.anchor: in v. 149 it is clear that the Israelites’ repentance is quick and unconditional.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses took up the Tablets after casting them down in anger.
rows.anchor: Moses took up the Tablets after previously casting them down in anger (v. 150).

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: The Tablets’ contents, namely the Torah, may be what is described as guidance and mercy, a description also used of the Quran.
rows.anchor: the contents of the Tablets—namely, the Torah—contained guidance and mercy (Ṭ, Z)—a description associated with both the Torah and the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nuskhah generally means a written copy, with a root sense of substitution, especially of a text.
rows.anchor: a word that generally denotes a written copy of something, but whose root meaning relates to substituting one thing for another, particularly as regards a text.

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Nuskhah may refer to new Tablets containing a copy of what was written on the originals.
rows.anchor: understand nuskhah as referring to new Tablets that Moses was given, which contained a “copy” of what had been inscribed on the originals (Q, R).

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Nuskhah may refer to guidance and mercy copied onto the Torah Tablets from the heavenly Preserved Tablet, the source of all Divine Revelation.
rows.anchor: guidance and mercy were inscribed upon, or copied onto, the Torah Tablets from the heavenly Preserved Tablet (see 85:22c), from which all Divine Revelation derives (Q).
